sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Sorting and searching questions appear in every fresher coding round. Either as theory ('explain bubble sort') or as a live problem ('find the first duplicate'). The two-pointer and frequency-count patterns solve 80% of fresher coding problems.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
**Two patterns dominate fresher coding problems:**

1. **Frequency count** — use a dict to count occurrences. Solves: duplicates, most-common, anagram check.
2. **Two pointers** — one from left, one from right. Solves: palindrome check, sorted-array sum pair, reverse.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Bubble sort** — O(n²) average/worst. Swap adjacent elements. Can you code it from memory in 10 lines?
- **`sorted()` vs `.sort()`** — `sorted()` returns a new list; `.sort()` mutates in place. Both accept `key=` and `reverse=True`.
- **Binary search** — O(log n) but requires sorted input. Middle element → recurse left or right.
- **Linear search** — O(n). The `in` operator on a list is a linear search. On a set/dict it's O(1).
- **Frequency map pattern** — `from collections import Counter; Counter(lst)` in one line.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **'What is the time complexity of Python's built-in sort?'** — O(n log n), Timsort algorithm.
- **'What is the precondition for binary search?'** — the list must be sorted. Missing this is the most common fresher mistake.
- **'Find duplicates in a list'** — frequency map with dict or set.
- **'Reverse a string in Python'** — `s[::-1]` or `''.join(reversed(s))`.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"My first instinct for most fresher array problems is the frequency-count pattern — build a dict of value→count in O(n), then answer the question in O(1). For sorted-array problems I look for two pointers. Only if those don't fit do I consider a nested-loop O(n²) solution, and I flag the complexity immediately."*
